title: How to Read a Parable
hook: Why did Jesus tell stories that confused even his own disciples?
tldr: Parables are not sermon illustrations; Jesus used them to hide truth from the hostile and draw seekers closer. Read them as first hearers did: Jewish listeners longing for God's reign on earth, steeped in Old Testament images, alert to jokes and twists. Use Jesus' own explanations, find the main point, and don't map every detail onto the afterlife.
big_idea: Hear the parable as its first audience did, not as an afterlife map.

points.title: Confusion is the invitation
points.text: Jesus said he spoke in parables so that some would see and not see (Luke 8:10). Jeremy Myers (Redeeming God): confusion is meant to send you to Jesus for an explanation.

points.title: Ask who first heard it
points.text: What matters is what the original audience heard: first-century Jews, their culture, how they read the Hebrew Bible, and the issues of their day, not ours.

points.title: The kingdom is God's reign on earth
points.text: Most parables are about the kingdom of God. Jesus' hearers did not think of heaven but of God's rule replacing Rome, here and now.

points.title: Old Testament imagery is the code
points.text: Furnaces, sons of men, harvests and shining righteous come from the prophets, especially Daniel. Without the Old Testament the parables are easy to misread.

points.title: Watch for jokes and twists
points.text: A careless sower, an enemy who bothers to sow weeds: Jesus told stories with a twinkle in his eye. The surprise usually carries the point, often aimed at the religious establishment.

points.title: Not every detail is a doctrine
points.text: Since Adolf Jülicher, scholars debate one point versus many. Most now allow several points but not that every detail stands for something, so story scenery is not an afterlife map.

sections.summary: Myers argues parables were told not to reveal truth but to conceal it. When the disciples asked why, Jesus said: so that in seeing they will not see, and in hearing they will not understand (Luke 8:10; Matthew 13:10-17, 34-35). The apostles, Jews who lived with him three years, were still confused and relieved when he spoke plainly (John 16:29). If they were confused, so may we be.

Myers laughs at Matthew 13:51: after a string of puzzling parables Jesus asks if they understood, and they answer, Yes, Lord! He suspects an Emperor's New Clothes moment, with no one brave enough to admit they had no clue. Anyone confident they understand all the parables, he says, should have their pride meter checked.

Some teaching was meant only for disciples and can be dangerous to people not ready for it; only those who practise what they have learned receive more (Luke 8:16-18). The parables also opened a door to discipleship: confused hearers who came to Jesus got an explanation. Hiding truth also kept the ruling class from understanding and crucifying him sooner.

Myers links the parables to Scripture as a whole: God does not want us to get life from a book, as the religious leaders tried to (John 5:39-40). Confusing parables push us to Jesus, the source of life. After many parables Jesus went out to heal and serve (Matthew 8-9), showing what they meant by leading people to love others.

Pastors say Jesus told stories, so we should too. Myers disagrees: stories illustrate a truth or help people remember it, while Jesus' parables were given to hide the point and make hearers ask. He also notes that most of the time Jesus taught through books of the Bible, so parables are no licence for nonsense sermons.

When Jesus explains some of the symbolism, as with the Four Soils and the Wheat and the Weeds, that is the first and best guide. Notice also what he leaves unexplained: in the wheat and weeds, the unexplained servants turn out to be the key to the parable.

sections.h: Key two: the first hearers' world
sections.summary: Myers: what matters most is not what we want a parable to say, but what the original audience heard. Learn their times and culture, how they read the Hebrew Bible, and what concerns filled their day. Kenneth Bailey, who studied village life in the Middle East, reads Luke's parables through peasant eyes and their poetic structures to recover unspoken assumptions.

Jesus had a sense of humour. Many stories were told with a twinkle in his eye and a half-smile: half-jokes, plays on words and surprising twists meant to amuse, delight and amaze. A sower flinging precious seed everywhere, an enemy sneaking in to plant weeds that grow anyway: the joke often carries the lesson.

sections.h: Kingdom of God: earth, not heaven
sections.summary: Most parables are about the kingdom of God, also called the kingdom of heaven. Today people hear heaven. Nobody in Jesus' day did: they suffered under the kingdom of Rome and longed for the Messiah to overthrow it. The kingdom is God's rule and reign on earth, here and now, replacing the kingdoms of men.

Jesus' hearers were nearly all Jews immersed in the Hebrew Scriptures from birth. Modern Christians who skip the Old Testament miss much of the New, especially the parables. In Matthew 13, for example, the furnace, the Son of Man and the shining righteous all come from Daniel 3, 7 and 12.

The parables were politically and religiously subversive, not mainly against Rome as people wanted, but against the politics and religion of Judaism's ruling class. Myers: if we miss the subversive, dangerous edge in a parable, we have likely misunderstood it.

Matthew 13 holds seven kingdom parables. Myers insists not one is about how to go to heaven when you die or how to tell if you are truly a Christian; all are about the nature, character, birth and growth of God's kingdom on earth. The same caution applies to parables that mention fire, darkness or Hades.

For centuries the church allegorized every detail. Adolf Jülicher insisted a parable makes only one main point and is not allegory. Klyne Snodgrass credits him but says he overcorrected: parables are expanded analogies meant to persuade and may teach several lessons, yet not every detail stands for something. Craig Blomberg suggests one point per main character.

sections.h: Doctrine reads parables, not the reverse
sections.summary: A Gospel Coalition article cites Tertullian's principle that doctrine should guide how we read parables, not the reverse, and recommends the parable's immediate context and the whole Bible as guides. Applied to hell, that means not building a detailed afterlife geography from story scenery such as the rich man's flames.

Matthew 13 opens with the Sower (Matthew 13:1-23; Luke 8:4-15), the longest and most important of the group, and one Jesus explains. Seed falls on four soils. Jesus names four responses to kingdom truth: some do not understand; some receive it with joy but fall away under trouble; some are lured away by life's cares and pleasures; some hold on and bear a great harvest.

sections.h: Four Soils: not saved versus unsaved
sections.summary: Many teach that only the fruitful fourth soil, or only the last three, have eternal life. Myers calls this a tragic mistake from confusing the kingdom of heaven with going to heaven. Saved in Luke 8:12 nearly always means rescue from a temporal problem. Luke's context stresses hearing and obeying (Luke 8:16-9:6). Anyone, believer or not, Pharisee, crowd or disciple, can be any soil.

sections.h: Four Soils: the twist and the lesson
sections.summary: The humour: seed was valuable, yet this sower scatters it willy-nilly. God is careless with kingdom truths, never caring much for efficiency. One life can hold all four soils, fruitful about some truths and hardened about others; discipleship tends the hard, rocky, thorny ground. Myers adds a twist: good soil is full of fertiliser, so the sinners churches keep out are rich ground. Bad people make good soil.

sections.h: Using this on the hell parables
sections.summary: Bring the same questions to every parable in this app. Who was listening, and what were they arguing about? What does Jesus himself explain? Which Old Testament scenes supply the fire, darkness or harvest? Where is the joke or twist, and whom does it unsettle? What is the main point about God's kingdom, and which details are simply the story's scenery?

steps.note: Crowd, disciples or Pharisees? What dispute or question sets up the story?

steps.note: Furnace, harvest, Son of Man, shining righteous: find where the prophets used them.

steps.label: Spot the joke or twist
steps.note: The surprising detail usually carries the point, often against the religious establishment.

steps.label: State the kingdom point
steps.note: What does it say about God's reign on earth? Don't turn scenery into afterlife doctrine.

mythfact.myth: Jesus told parables to make his teaching simple and clear.
mythfact.fact: Jesus said he spoke in parables so some would see and not see (Luke 8:10). Explanations went to those who came and asked.

mythfact.myth: The kingdom of heaven in the parables means heaven after death.
mythfact.fact: First-century Jews heard God's reign on earth replacing Rome. Myers: none of the Matthew 13 parables is about going to heaven when you die.

mythfact.myth: Every detail in a parable is a coded doctrine.
mythfact.fact: Since Jülicher, scholars reject allegorizing every detail. Even Snodgrass, who allows several points, says not every detail stands for something.

mythfact.myth: The Four Soils sorts true Christians from false ones.
mythfact.fact: Myers: it shows four responses to kingdom truth, and one person can be every soil about different truths.

terms.meaning: A short story comparing something to God's kingdom; for Myers, told to conceal truth and draw seekers to ask.
A story in which details stand for other things; debated as a way to read parables since Jülicher.
God's rule and reign on earth, here and now, replacing human kingdoms such as Rome.
Myers: nearly always rescue from a temporal problem such as sickness, enemies or sin, not only going to heaven.
Kenneth Bailey's method: early Middle Eastern interpretations and village culture used to recover what first hearers assumed.

quiz.q: According to Jesus, why did he speak in parables?
options: So some would see and not see
quiz.why: Luke 8:10 and Matthew 13:13-15: parables veiled truth, and explanations went to those who came asking.

quiz.q: What did first-century Jews mean by the kingdom of God?
options: God's reign on earth replacing Rome
quiz.why: They longed for the Messiah to overthrow Rome; the kingdom is God's rule on earth, here and now.

quiz.q: In Myers' reading, who can be each of the four soils?
options: Anyone, even one person about different truths
quiz.why: The soils are responses to kingdom truths; one life can be fruitful soil on some and hard ground on others.

reflect: Which parable have you read as an afterlife map that might really be about God's kingdom on earth?

objections.claim: Jesus told parables to make truth clearer, like any good teacher. The idea that he meant to confuse is backwards.
objections.strongest: Mark 4:33 says Jesus spoke the word as they were able to hear it. Parables use everyday images precisely to make the unfamiliar accessible, and crowds plainly grasped some of them, as the leaders did in Matthew 21:45.
objections.response: Both are true for different hearers. Jesus himself says parables hide truth from some (Luke 8:10; Matthew 13:13-15), and Mark 4:34 adds that he explained everything privately to his disciples. Myers' point is that the veil is an invitation: those who come asking receive more (Luke 8:16-18). When the leaders understood a parable, it was because it was aimed at them, and they wanted to arrest him, which shows why Jesus often kept the subversive point veiled.

objections.claim: Jesus himself decodes details, so the fire, darkness and torment in parables must be read as literal descriptions of hell.
objections.strongest: Snodgrass shows Jülicher's one-point rule fails: Jesus' own explanations match many details to realities. If the weeds are people and the reapers angels, consistency says the furnace is a real place of punishment.
objections.response: Granting several correspondences is not the same as making every image literal. Snodgrass himself says parables are not allegories in which every detail stands for something. Jesus decodes characters, but he does not say the furnace is an afterlife place; that image already exists in Daniel 3. Reading Old Testament imagery and the first audience's concerns, as Myers urges, is how we tell a decoded symbol from story scenery. Tertullian's rule points the same way: build doctrine from clear teaching, then read parables.

objections.claim: The Four Soils clearly separates true believers from false professors; only the fruitful soil is genuinely saved.
objections.strongest: Luke 8:12 says the devil takes the word so they may not believe and be saved. The rocky and thorny soils show enthusiasm without genuine conversion and profession without perseverance; only the good soil endures and bears fruit.
objections.response: Myers answers that saved in the Gospels usually means rescue from a present trouble, and Luke's context is about hearing and obeying (Luke 8:16-21), as the wind, demons and a sick woman obey Jesus. Jesus saw all four responses in Pharisees, crowds and his own disciples. Because there are many kingdom truths, one person can be fruitful on some and hardened on others. Using the parable to sort eternal destinies, he argues, has caused great harm.

objections.claim: Reading parables through modern Middle Eastern village culture is anachronistic guesswork.
objections.strongest: Bailey's critics note his key assumption, that present Middle Eastern peasant culture is archaic and accurately reflects Jesus' world, cannot be proven, and some of his readings clash with long-standing interpretations.
objections.response: The caution is fair, and village observation should be checked against ancient evidence. But the core claim, that we must hear parables as first-century Jews did, does not depend on Bailey alone. Myers grounds it in the Hebrew Scriptures they knew, their longing for God to replace Rome, and the disputes in the text itself, such as the Beelzebub clash before Matthew 13. Those anchors are ancient and in the Bible.
